Staffing fairness and barriers: 2025 survey

What federal employees reported about staffing fairness, bias, assessment and accommodation in the 2025 Staffing and Non-Partisanship Survey (SNPS). These results describe respondents across organizations subject to the Public Service Employment Act. They are not results for any one department.

There were 82,987 respondents, a response rate of 30.9%. Surveyed June 5 to August 14, 2025. Questions about past staffing experiences generally refer to April 1, 2024 through March 31, 2025. Results are adjusted for non-response. PSC 2025 report ↗

Good practice for presenting equity data

  • Name the source and the date of each figure.
  • Compare an organization with its own workforce availability where Treasury Board publishes it, and with the public service.
  • Show subgroups separately where their results are published. A combined result can hide a gap for one subgroup.
  • Keep suppressed values suppressed. A suppressed value is not zero.
  • Say what the data do not show, such as the cause of a difference.
  • Check the figures against your organization’s own records before you share them.

How to read what you see

Five conventions apply to most charts and tables in this tool.

  • In bar charts, the bar is the result and the short vertical line is the comparison point, usually workforce availability. A bar that stops before the line is below the comparison point; a bar that goes past it is above.
  • Red means below the comparison point and green means at or above it. A red result is not a conclusion on its own.
  • A ratio of 1.0 means a group received exactly its proportional share, for example of promotions or of a salary band. Below 1.0 means less than its share; above 1.0 means more.
  • "supp." marks a suppressed count. A count of 1 to 5 people is not published, to protect privacy. It is not zero.
  • Percentages are a group’s share. For example, "23.9% racialized" means that 23.9% of employees self-identified as members of a visible minority.

Labels show where each number comes from:

official data taken directly from Treasury Board, the Public Service Commission or the survey.   computed a ratio, gap or ranking calculated from official figures.   you enter values you type into a calculator.

How to find where barriers may exist

Six steps, in order, for a group or an organization.

  1. Start with the employment cycle table in the Overview. It shows where each group’s share falls below a benchmark: in the workforce, in hiring, in promotions, among executives, in pay or in separations.
  2. Compare an organization with its own workforce availability, in Department data. Treasury Board publishes availability for each organization, based on its occupations and regions.
  3. Look at subgroups. A combined result can hide a gap for First Nations, Métis or Inuit employees, for Black employees or another racialized community, or for one type of disability.
  4. Read the employee survey results for the same group: harassment, discrimination, respect and confidence in recourse. When a gap in representation and a gap in workplace experience concern the same group, they point to the same place.
  5. Note what is missing: suppressed values, and data that are not published, such as acting appointments by group. Use the request builder to ask for them.
  6. Write down the source and date of each figure, and present it with what the data cannot show. The presentation and briefing note tools do this for you.

How results are marked on this site
  • Representation: red marks a share below the workforce availability used for comparison. Each organization is compared with its own availability where Treasury Board publishes it.
  • Employment cycle and pay: a ratio compares a group with a benchmark, and 1.00 means the same rate. A ratio of 0.85 or less is marked, and for separations a ratio of 1.15 or more. The salary index marks 0.85 or less in the upper salary ranges and 1.15 or more in the lower ranges.
  • Employee survey: differences are in percentage points between published percentages. Some tables mark differences of 3 points or more that are less favourable for a group.
  • Each mark comes with a symbol or a word as well as a colour. Marks are a screening rule that shows where to look more closely. They are not tests of statistical significance or legal standards, and they do not show the cause of a difference.

Cautions
  1. Each organization has its own workforce availability, which reflects its occupations and locations. This site compares each organization with its own availability where Treasury Board publishes it. A gap shows where to look further. It is not a conclusion on its own.
  2. Self-identification is voluntary, so representation may be higher than shown.
  3. Departmental promotions, acting appointments, subgroup figures by department and detailed survey results by department are published in interactive federal dashboards. This tool links to them.

Overview

This site presents published Government of Canada data on employment equity in the federal public service. It covers the four designated groups under the Employment Equity Act and their subgroups: representation, hiring, promotion, pay, leadership and employee survey results. Figures are reproduced from the published sources. Where a figure is calculated or estimated, the section says so. Results that a source suppresses to protect privacy remain suppressed.

Selected results for the public service official data

Each result links to the section that presents the data and its source.

  1. Persons with disabilities are 9.0% of employees, compared with workforce availability of 12.0%. This is the only designated group below its workforce availability. See Equity groups and subgroups.
  2. Racialized employees are 23.9% of the workforce and 17.3% of executives. Black employees are 5.1% of the workforce and 3.2% of executives. See Executives and leadership.
  3. In 2025, the disproportionality index for Black employees was 1.46 in the lowest salary range and 0.63 in the highest. Their estimated median salary was $10,450 below the median for all employees, compared with $4,100 in 2017 (estimates by the Disproportionality Index project). See the salary disproportionality index.
  4. In the Public Service Commission audit of recruitment, persons with disabilities were 4.4% of applicants and 2.4% of appointments. Black candidates were 10.3% of applicants and 6.6% of appointments. See Hiring, promotion and separation.
  5. In the 2024 Public Service Employee Survey, 9% of employees said they had been a victim of discrimination in the past 12 months. Of those, 75% said it came from individuals with authority over them, and 53% took no action. 11% of employees who experienced race-based discrimination were satisfied with how racism complaints are resolved. See Employee survey.
  6. The share of employees earning $100,000 or more is 41.5% for all employees, 47.4% for Chinese employees, 28.5% for Black employees and 21.4% for Filipino employees. See Salary and pay equity.
This site includes the published Treasury Board tables on representation by department, subgroups, salary, hiring, promotion, separations, executives, regions, occupations and official languages, and the public-service-wide 2024 PSES results for the equity questions. Departmental promotions, acting appointments, applicant data by subgroup and detailed PSES results are published in interactive federal dashboards, and each section links to the relevant dashboard. For help using the site, see How to use this tool.

Representation in all organizations

Representation of the four designated groups in each organization of the core public administration, March 31, 2025, compared with each organization’s own workforce availability. The core public administration is the set of organizations for which the Treasury Board is the employer, listed in Schedules I and IV of the Financial Administration Act. Separate agencies, such as the Canada Revenue Agency, publish their own reports; links are in Data sources.

Hiring, promotions and separations

Representation at each stage of recruitment

The Public Service Commission’s Audit of Employment Equity Representation in Recruitment followed 15,285 applications to 181 externally advertised processes in 30 organizations through five hiring stages. The survival ratio is representation at the appointment stage divided by representation at the application stage. A ratio of 1.00 means the group’s share was the same at both stages; below 1.00 means its share was lower at appointment.

Representation at each recruitment stage (audit sample, processes closing 2016-17, published 2021). Source: PSC audit, Annex B.
GroupApplicationAutomated screeningOrganizational screeningAssessmentAppointmentSurvival ratio
Women52.8%53.2%59.7%59.8%58.2%1.10
Indigenous Peoples3.5%3.6%4.0%2.9%2.9%0.83
Persons with disabilities4.4%4.7%4.5%3.6%2.4%0.55
Members of visible minorities30.4%30.3%27.4%24.6%24.7%0.81
Black candidates10.3%9.7%7.7%6.3%6.6%0.64
Chinese candidates3.4%3.5%4.2%3.2%3.5%1.03
Non-white West Asian, North African or Arab4.6%4.4%3.8%4.2%3.3%0.72
South Asian / East Indian5.6%5.8%5.0%5.2%5.9%1.05

The audit reported results for each stage. Automated screening did not reduce any group’s representation. Organizational screening reduced the representation of racialized candidates, and of Black candidates the most; the audit identified citizenship status and the assessment of experience as factors, and found that visible minority candidates were less successful even when they had federal experience. At assessment, written tests, mostly developed by organizations, open-ended and scored subjectively, reduced the representation of racialized candidates, and of Black candidates in particular. Interviews accounted for the decline for Indigenous candidates. Reference checks increased representation only for women. The appointment stage reduced the representation of persons with disabilities, their largest decline at any stage. The 2023 follow-up audit on pre-assessment found that screening also reduced the representation of Indigenous people with disabilities and racialized people with disabilities. 50% of organizations had completed an employment systems review in the previous 3 to 5 years, and 62% of those concluded that they had no systemic barriers in recruitment.

Promotions and acting appointments

Acting appointments are not reported in Treasury Board tables. The Public Service Commission subgroup dashboard reports employees, promotions and acting appointments by group and subgroup for each organization. Enter your organization’s figures here to calculate the promotion ratio and the acting ratio. Comparing the two ratios shows whether a difference appears in acting appointments, in promotions, or in both.

Compare one group across organizations

Choose a group and a question to see that group’s result in every organization that published it, ranked, with the group’s public-service result marked. For example, it shows the organizations where Black employees report the lowest trust in recourse.

Smaller organizations have fewer respondents in each group, so a single organization’s result can change with a few responses. Results for the public service and for larger organizations are more stable.

Two groups compared

Choose two groups to see their results on the same questions side by side, for the public service, with the difference. For example, compare Black employees and non-racialized employees on feeling safe to speak about racism.

Employee support services and outcomes

This page covers employee support services: ombuds offices, employee networks, informal conflict management systems, and anti-racism or inclusion teams. It presents findings from federal evaluations of informal conflict management and a cost calculator. The 2024 survey results on harassment, discrimination and recourse are in the Employee survey section.

How to read this

  • The bar shows the actual result.
  • The tick or benchmark shows the comparison point.

Context

These survey results describe employees’ views of recourse and support. They do not count the cases brought to formal or informal processes.

Check next

Employee survey · Demographic gaps · Missing data · Use these figures in a briefing note or request →

What these services are

An ombuds office is an independent, impartial, confidential and informal channel for raising and resolving concerns outside the chain of command. Employee networks bring together employees from equity-seeking groups and provide a channel to senior management. Section 207 of the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act requires every deputy head in the core public administration to establish an informal conflict management system. An anti-racism or inclusion, diversity, equity and accessibility (IDEA) team is a unit with staff assigned to this work. The survey results below relate to all of these services.

Raising issues and recourse, 2024 survey

Public-service-wide results from the 2024 Public Service Employee Survey. The same results appear in the Employee survey section.

Section 207 of the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act requires every deputy head in the core public administration, in consultation with bargaining agents, to establish an informal conflict management system and to inform employees that it is available. Section 5 of the Employment Equity Act requires employers to identify and eliminate employment barriers against persons in designated groups. Part II of the Canada Labour Code sets out obligations for the prevention of workplace hazards, including harassment and violence.

Cost calculator you enter

This calculator estimates costs from values you enter. Starting values come from the evaluations above: the share of a manager’s time spent on conflict, and a replacement cost of 150% of compensation. The default cost per employee, $125,000, is the Parliamentary Budget Officer’s average personnel cost per full-time equivalent (salary plus standard compensation; the PBO reports total federal personnel spending of $71.1 billion in 2024-25). Average base salary in the public service is about $100,000 (Treasury Board). Replace any value with your organization’s figures. The calculation includes two direct effects: time recovered from unresolved conflict, and the difference in cost when a matter is resolved informally rather than formally. Indirect effects, such as turnover, sick leave and legal costs, are not included. Results are estimates, not official figures.

All values can be changed. Using your organization’s grievance counts, informal conflict management data and salary information makes the estimate specific to your organization.

Read with care

  • Each dot is an organization. A pattern across organizations does not tell you what any one employee experienced.

Representation and changes in the benchmark

Representation is compared with workforce availability, the benchmark used under the Employment Equity Act. From the March 31, 2024 data, Treasury Board bases workforce availability on the 2021 Census and the 2022 Canadian Survey on Disability. For racialized (visible minority) employees, the benchmark rose from 17.3% to 22.7%. An organization’s representation can rise while its gap to the updated benchmark also grows. This page explains the change and how to describe results.

How to read this

  • The bar shows the actual result.
  • The tick or benchmark shows the comparison point.
  • A gap is the difference between a result and its benchmark.
  • Suppressed data means the count is too small to publish. It does not mean zero.
  • Read this with related data before drawing conclusions.

Context

Representation can rise while the gap to the benchmark grows, when the benchmark itself changes. Compare the gap as well as the number of employees.

Check next

Overview · Salary DI tracker · Demographic gaps · Use these figures in a briefing note or request →

What changed in the benchmark official data

  • The benchmark for equitable representation is workforce availability (WFA), the share of the workforce, in occupations matching the public service, that belongs to each group.
  • From the March 31, 2022 data, workforce availability counts permanent residents as well as Canadian citizens. Earlier estimates based on the 2016 Census counted Canadian citizens only. From the March 31, 2024 data, it is based on the 2021 Census and the 2022 Canadian Survey on Disability.
  • For racialized employees, workforce availability was 15.3% based on the 2016 Census (citizens only), 17.2% for 2022 and 17.3% for 2023 (2016 Census, citizens and permanent residents), and 22.7% for 2024 and 2025 (2021 Census). Because the benchmark changed, a change in representation from one year to the next is read against the benchmark in effect for each year.
  • Representation and the gap to the current benchmark can move in opposite directions. Both are shown below.

Representation of racialized employees compared with the current benchmark

Representation of racialized employees in each organization, compared with workforce availability of 22.7% for the public service. Results below the benchmark are shown in red. Use the lists to sort the organizations or to show one size category.

How to describe the results

If an organization’s representation of racialized employees rose but remains below 22.7%, representation increased and a gap to workforce availability remains. If representation rose and the benchmark rose more, the gap grew. An organization whose result is further below the new benchmark than the old one has not necessarily lost representation, because the benchmark changed.

Sources: Treasury Board of Canada Secretariat, employment-equity representation and workforce-availability estimates (2021 Census and 2022 Canadian Survey on Disability, citizens and permanent residents, as of March 31, 2024 and 2025). The benchmark change is documented in TBS employment-equity reporting. Independent analytical tool.

Methodology and audit trail

Figures in this tool come from published sources, mainly from the Government of Canada. Where a figure is calculated or estimated, this is stated. This page records, for each dataset, its source, how it was processed, and what it can and cannot support, so the work can be checked and reproduced.

Principles

  • Numbers are copied verbatim from official tables. Where a value was derived (for example, summing salary bands), the calculation is noted and was checked against published totals.
  • Suppressed cells are left suppressed. They are never estimated, interpolated or filled.
  • No organization's data is matched to a different organization. Where a name could not be matched across datasets, the cell is left blank.
  • Survey differences and correlations show where to look further. They do not establish causes.

TopicPublished resultsQuestion to examine
Discrimination and feeling valued at workIn 2024, 15% of Black employees and 16% of Indigenous employees reported being a victim of discrimination, compared with 9% of all employees. 69% of Black employees said they feel valued at work, compared with 67% of all employees. Among persons with disabilities, 21% reported discrimination and 59% said they feel valued at work.Are discrimination results reviewed by group, separately from engagement results such as feeling valued at work?

First official language and language training48.5% of Black employees have French as their first official language, compared with 30.2% of all employees. 36% of Black employees and 34% of all employees said lack of access to second-language training adversely affected their career progress.How is language training allocated across groups and levels in the organization?
Persons with disabilitiesPersons with disabilities are the only designated group below workforce availability (9.0% compared with 12.0%). Implementation of accommodation fell from 81% in 2019 to 71% in 2024, and requests for accommodation rose from 13% in 2022 to 19% in 2024. Disability as a type of discrimination cited rose from 19% to 26% between 2022 and 2024, the largest increase of any type. Their share of separations rose from 6.6% in 2021-22 to 8.7% in 2024-25, and their share of hires rose from 5.5% to 8.6% over the same years.How long does it take to implement accommodation, and how does this compare with separations of persons with disabilities?
Promotions and acting appointmentsAcross the public service, the promotion share of each of the four designated groups meets or exceeds its workforce share. Acting appointments are not reported in Treasury Board tables; the Public Service Commission dashboard reports them. Occupational categoriesWomen are 74.0% of administrative support, 21.7% of operational services and 7.2% of electronics. Trust and data qualitySelf-identification is voluntary. The 2024 survey response rate was 50.5%.What are the organization’s self-identification completion rates, and how have they changed?
Assessment in recruitmentThe Public Service Commission recruitment audit found that automated screening did not reduce any group’s representation. Written tests reduced the representation of racialized candidates, and of Black candidates in particular. Interviews accounted for the decline for Indigenous candidates. Reference checks increased representation only for women. The appointment decision reduced the representation of persons with disabilities. 88% of candidates with disabilities did not request assessment accommodation, and 12% of organizations required at least one employment equity group member on assessment boards.Which assessment tools did the organization use in its recent staffing processes, and are results tracked by group at each stage?
Employment systems reviewsIn the Public Service Commission audit, 50% of audited organizations had completed an employment systems review in the previous 3 to 5 years, and 62% of those concluded that they had no systemic barriers in recruitment. The same audit found declines in representation at specific stages of recruitment for three of the four designated groups.How do the conclusions of the organization’s last employment systems review compare with its results in this site?

Compare two measures across organizations

This is a scatter plot. Choose one measure for the horizontal axis and another for the vertical axis. Each dot is one organization. If the dots rise from bottom left to top right, the two measures tend to increase together. If they fall from top left to bottom right, one tends to decrease as the other increases. A scattered cloud means there is no clear relationship. The r value summarizes this from -1 to +1, where 0 means no linear relationship. The chart shows whether two measures vary together across organizations, and which organizations are far from the overall pattern. It does not show that one measure causes the other.

Organizations below a representation threshold

Choose a group and a number of percentage points below workforce availability for the public service. The list shows every organization at or beyond that threshold, with a summary you can copy into a briefing note. Each organization’s own workforce availability may differ from the public-service figure.

Data files

The Public Service Commission dashboard draws on the Treasury Board Employment Equity Data Bank (EEDB), matched with the Commission’s hiring and staffing activity files. Machine-readable releases are published on the Open Government portal and canada.ca. Each family of files is listed below with its location. The tool at the bottom of the page opens an official CSV file in your browser; nothing is uploaded.

Salary disproportionality index, 2017 to 2025

The Disproportionality Index (DI) compares a group’s presence in a salary range with that of all employees. A DI of 1.0 means a group is in that salary range at the same rate as all employees. Above 1.0 means overrepresented in that range; below 1.0 means underrepresented. These are the published figures of the independent Disproportionality Index project, derived from Treasury Board diversity and inclusion statistics.

How to read this

  • The bar shows the actual result.
  • The tick or benchmark shows the comparison point.
  • A gap is the difference between a result and its benchmark.
  • Suppressed data means the count is too small to publish. It does not mean zero.
  • Read this with related data before drawing conclusions.

Context

An index above 1.0 in lower ranges and below 1.0 in higher ranges means that a group is concentrated in lower salaries.

Check next

Salary · Hiring and promotion · Executives · Use these figures in a briefing note or request →

DI for a group in a salary range = (that group's % in the range) ÷ (all employees' % in the same range). Example from the source: in 2024, 34.78% of Black employees and 23.87% of all employees earned salaries in the lowest range, giving a DI of 34.78 ÷ 23.87 = 1.46. Salary ranges shift from year to year because they track the median, and the source sets new ranges each year. This is why the range labels below change with the year you choose.

Data sources

This list comes from the Data Equity page on GCwiki. Each card describes what the source contains and what it can be used for.

About the data

Definitions

Core public administration (CPA)
The 72 organizations where Treasury Board is the employer. Separate agencies such as CRA, CFIA, NRC and Parks Canada have their own reports.
Workforce availability (WFA)
The estimated share of each designated group in the Canadian workforce who could be recruited into public service jobs, based on the 2021 Census and the 2022 Canadian Survey on Disability. It is the benchmark used under the Employment Equity Act. Treasury Board states that it should be regarded as a starting point.
Representation
The share of employees who have voluntarily self-identified with a group. Because self-identification is voluntary, true numbers may be higher than reported.
Designated groups
Women, Indigenous Peoples, persons with disabilities, and members of visible minorities (racialized employees), as set in the Employment Equity Act. Treasury Board reports Black employees separately, as a subgroup of members of visible minorities. There is no workforce availability for Black employees because the Act does not designate the subgroup.
Suppression
Counts of 1 to 5 people are not shown in published tables, to protect privacy. They appear here as "supp." A suppressed cell is not zero.
Promotion equity ratio
A group's share of promotions divided by its share of the workforce. Below 1.0 means the group receives fewer promotions than its size predicts.
Disproportionality ratio
A group’s share in a salary band divided by all employees’ share in the same band. Above 1.0 in low bands and below 1.0 in high bands means the group is concentrated in lower pay.
Acting appointment
Temporarily performing the duties of a higher-level position.

Limits of this tool

Figures were transcribed on June 11, 2026 from tables published by the Treasury Board of Canada Secretariat in the Employment Equity Annual Report 2024-25 and its Demographic Snapshot, and from the Treasury Board representation and workforce availability series. Six-band salary counts were produced by adding Treasury Board’s published detailed bands and were checked against published totals. Departmental workforce availability, departmental promotions and acting appointments, applicant data, subgroup figures by department and detailed PSES results are published in interactive federal dashboards and are linked, not copied. Each department has its own workforce availability, which reflects its occupations and regions and is available in the Public Service Commission dashboard. The 12.0% workforce availability for persons with disabilities is based on the definition used in the Canadian Survey on Disability, which is broader than the definition used in the self-identification questionnaire. Separations include retirements. Related legislation and policy: Employment Equity Act, section 5 (duty to identify and eliminate barriers), Canadian Human Rights Act, the Clerk’s Call to Action, and the Canadian Human Rights Commission’s horizontal audit of the employment of racialized people in management and executive positions (2025).

Definitions in plain language

The terms used in this tool, in plain language. The technical term is shown in parentheses where it differs.

Employment equity
A legal duty to identify and remove barriers so the workforce reflects the people available to do the work, for the four designated groups.
Designated group
The four groups named in the Employment Equity Act: women, Indigenous Peoples, persons with disabilities, and members of visible minorities (racialized employees).
Subgroup
A more specific group within a designated group, such as First Nations, Métis or Inuit within Indigenous Peoples, or Black employees within racialized employees.
Workforce availability (WFA)
The share of a group in the Canadian workforce available for these jobs, based on the census. It is the benchmark used under the Act. Treasury Board states that it should be regarded as a starting point.
Benchmark
The comparison point a result is measured against. Here it is usually workforce availability.
Representation
The share of employees who have voluntarily self-identified with a group. Because it is voluntary, the true number may be higher.
Representation gap
Representation minus the benchmark, in percentage points. A negative gap means the group is below the level the available workforce would predict.
Suppression
When a count is too small to publish (often 1 to 5 people), it is withheld to protect privacy. A suppressed cell is not zero.
Ratio
One share divided by another. Below 1.0 means less than expected; above 1.0 means more than expected.
Disproportionality index
A group's share within a salary band compared with its share of the whole workforce. Above 1.0 means over-represented in that band; below 1.0, under-represented.
Core public administration (CPA)
The roughly 72 organizations where the Treasury Board is the employer. Separate agencies such as the CRA or Parks Canada report on their own.
Public service
The broader federal public service, including separate agencies. Wider than the core public administration.
Department
A federal organization. Here, an employer covered by the data, used interchangeably with organization.
Public Service Employee Survey (PSES)
A confidential survey of federal employees on their workplace experience, run every one to two years.
Hiring
Bringing a person into a job from outside or through a staffing process, measured here at stages from application to appointment.
Promotion
Moving to a higher-level position. A main path for career progression.
Executive (EX)
The senior leadership group (EX classifications), below the deputy head level.
EX feeder group
The levels just below executive (often EX minus 1 and EX minus 2) from which most executives are drawn.
Self-identification
Voluntarily telling the employer that you belong to a designated group. It is how representation is counted.
Disaggregated data
Data broken down into smaller categories, such as by group, subgroup, level, branch or region, rather than reported as one total.

Limitations of the data

What this public data can and cannot show. Read this before drawing conclusions.

The results describe differences between groups and between organizations. They do not show the cause of a difference, and they do not show that discrimination occurred.

What this data does not show

  • Public datasets may not show process-level barriers (who decided what, and how).
  • Suppressed values do not mean zero; they mean the count was too small to publish.
  • Self-identification is voluntary, so representation may understate the true numbers.
  • A department's own workforce availability may differ from the public-service-wide benchmark, reflecting its occupations and region.
  • Data may not include branch, region, classification, occupational group, language profile, security level, or process stage.
  • Some questions require additional departmental data before conclusions can be drawn.
